title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Problem II of E410 asks for the 'velaria', the shape of a perfectly flexible, weightless thread of uniform thickness exposed to a horizontal wind. The axis AX is horizontal and parallel to the wind. The wind meets the element ds at angle 90°−φ.

Force law (end of §XXVI): following the Newtonian impact rule, the wind force on ds equals the weight of an air column of base ds and height k·cos²φ, where k is the height due to the wind speed. Euler only needs proportionality, so the load is purely normal: tangential load p ds = 0 and normal load q ds = −β ds cos²φ (sign because it acts opposite to his positive normal).

§XXVII: this is again his 'first case', a perfectly flexible line with no bending moment. The equilibrium equations are dT = p ds and T dφ = −q ds. They give:
(I) dT = 0, so T = C, i.e. constant tension.
(II) C dφ = β ds cos²φ.

Integrating C dφ/cos²φ = β ds gives C tanφ = βs + D. With tanφ = dx/dy this is C dx/dy = βs + D. That is the intrinsic equation of the catenary of the previous problem, with the axis now horizontal instead of vertical.

Cartesian form: multiply by sinφ and use ds sinφ = dx. This gives C/cosφ = βx + D', where Euler silently reuses the letter D for this new constant. With cosφ = dy/ds this becomes C ds = (βx + D) dy. Then dy = C dx/√((βx+D)² − C²) and βs = √((βx+D)² − C²) + E.

On the next page, choosing the origin where the tangent is perpendicular to the wind gives C = D = βa. Hence dy = a dx/√(2ax + x²), y = a ln((x + a + √(2ax+x²))/a) and s = √(2ax+x²). This is a common catenary with constant tension βa.
errors: The letter D is used for two different integration constants: in C tanφ = βs + D and in C/cosφ = βx + D. These are independent constants in general. They coincide (both equal C) only with the normalization adopted on the next page, so the reuse is harmless but sloppy.

The physical model (Newtonian impact force ∝ sin² of the incidence angle, with the air streaming past) is an assumption. Other wind models, e.g. uniform normal pressure, give a circle instead. Euler explicitly sets the issue aside ('quicquid autem sit'). This is a modelling choice, not a mathematical error.

ideas.what: Velaria (sail curve) under a normal wind load ∝ cos²φ is a catenary; the tension is constant along the thread
ideas.modern_name: velaria / catenary equivalence under Newtonian impact pressure
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jakob Bernoulli and Johann Bernoulli (1690s, Acta Eruditorum)
ideas.where_published: E410 itself; the problem is classical and is also treated in Euler's mechanics writings, discussed by Truesdell, 'The Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638–1788'

ideas.what: Intrinsic equilibrium equations of a flexible line with tangential and normal distributed loads (dT = p ds, T dφ = −q ds)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Johann Bernoulli / Euler (general form); Euler's systematic use in E410 noted by Truesdell
ideas.where_published: E410, earlier sections; Truesdell's commentary in Opera omnia II.11/2

ideas.what: Reduction of the intrinsic equation C tanφ = βs + D to Cartesian quadrature via multiplication by sinφ
ideas.modern_name: first integral / quadrature of the catenary
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard (Leibniz, Huygens, Johann Bernoulli 1691 for the catenary)
ideas.where_published: E410; also the catenary treatment in E65 (Methodus inveniendi) appendix context

deep.surprise_reason: This is a textbook re-derivation of the Bernoulli result that the velaria under Newtonian wind pressure is a catenary, used as an illustration of Euler's general intrinsic equations. It is well documented in Truesdell's history; nothing new.
transcription_corrections: The section number at 'Quare quum hoc problema...' reads XXVII in the image, not XXVIII. The next section, on page 400, is XXVIII.
In 'II°. vero Cdφ = βds.cos.φ²' the image confirms this; the earlier 'q ds = − β ds. cos. φ²' is likewise correct as transcribed.
